doc.title: Oliver Nelson Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 10, 2020

chapter: Sound Pieces and Los Angeles studios
title: Studio musicians, the Fender bass and television pay
summary: Sheridon Stokes and tympani, Carol Kaye, studio pay, 3000 dollars a show over 26 weeks, and his father's income.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Oh no, no, no, no, no. You really wouldn’t. But you know what he tried to conduct, and he found guys that would really work well with him. So actually I was talking — who

was I talking to — oh it was Sheridon Stokes is a flute player. And he did some stuff in California with Dad and one time he said well they needed somebody to play tympani. Well Dad went back and played the tympani. So you do whatever it takes to make the deal work. I mean there was a lot of different interesting people. Carol Kaye, a member of the Rat Pack, Carol Kaye that did all the stuff — well he’d write parts out for Fender bass. He called her “Fender Bass” and he’d have parts for her to play the Fender bass on. But it was an interesting time because Ray Brown had a bass in every studio. The horn players, Bud Shank and those guys, they had a cartage service and they would actually have this service come and pick their instruments up and take it to the next studio. So they didn’t even lug horns anymore. And I mean they were making pretty — I mean you make 250, 300 bucks for four hours, then you go to another studio and you do that. And I always tell my students, we talk about how much guys for television make today. Dad was making about 3000 dollars a show. And it was a 26-week season back then so it was a lot longer than it is today.
Three thousand a show, what is that, how is that divided up into services?
So you’d come and you’d write the music and you’d conduct the music and they’d have a check drawn for three grand.

And so you’d have 26 of those three grands going. And then they’d have him do other projects. So then he had the jazz stuff he was still doing, plus he was doing — he was actually making 250 to 300 thousand dollars a year back in the 70s. So he was doing real well —
No he was doing real well and he needed to turn some stuff down but he didn’t. He just wanted to keep that whole ship running because you never know when it’s going to dry out.
